prompt: Give me a comprehensive overview of the history of New Zealand's national parks.

response.response_text:
# The History of New Zealand's National Parks

New Zealand's national parks are among the country's most treasured taonga (treasures) — a network of protected landscapes stretching from the volcanic plateau of the central North Island to the remote fiords of the deep south. Their story is one of Māori generosity, settler conservation instincts, legislative milestones, and an evolving understanding of what it means to protect the natural world. [[1]](cite://1/1)

![embed-1](embed://1)

## The First National Park: A Gift from Ngāti Tūwharetoa

The origins of New Zealand's national park system lie in an extraordinary act of rangatiratanga (chiefly authority) in 1887. Tūwharetoa paramount chief Horonuku Te Heuheu was facing a real threat: different tribes were disputing ownership of the volcanic peaks of Ruapehu, Ngāuruhoe and Tongariro, and there was a danger they would be divided and sold to Pākehā settlers. [[2]](cite://2/1)

Horonuku's response was to sign a deed with the Crown, ensuring the mountains could never be sold. As he put it: "Tongariro is my ancestor, my tupuna; it is my head; my mana centres around Tongariro." [[3]](cite://3/1) The government subsequently purchased additional Māori land to supplement the mountaintops, and Tongariro National Park was formally established by an 1894 act of Parliament — making it New Zealand's first national park, and one of the earliest in the world. [[2]](cite://2/2)

The park is today a dual World Heritage Site, recognised for both its cultural and natural significance. [[4]](cite://4/1)

## Early Expansion: The Turn of the 20th Century

The creation of Tongariro sparked momentum. By 1900, national parks had also been established on Taranaki (Mt Egmont) — the forest around the mountain had been protected by a reserve as early as 1875, with the area within six miles of the summit formally gazetted as the country's second national park in 1900. [[5]](cite://5/1) Large areas of South Island mountain lands were also set aside at Aoraki/Mt Cook and Arthur's Pass, and almost a million hectares was reserved in Fiordland in 1905. [[5]](cite://5/2)

The motivations behind this early wave of protection were mixed. Some settlers were alarmed that clearing forest for farms was destroying scenic landscapes; a few scientists worried about the loss of native plants and wildlife; and the government was increasingly aware of the tourism potential of New Zealand's natural wonders. [[6]](cite://6/1)

Conservationist Harry Ell was a key figure of this era. His persistent advocacy in Parliament led to the Scenery Preservation Act of 1903, which established a commission to investigate which areas were suitable for preservation. By the time Ell left Parliament, more than 500 reserves had been created nationwide — many of which, such as those at Aoraki/Mt Cook and in the Paparoa Range, later formed the basis of future national parks. [[7]](cite://7/1)

## Tourism, Recreation and Early Management

Until the 1940s, New Zealand's national parks were managed primarily as places for recreation and tourism, following the American model that prioritised visitor pleasure over nature conservation. [[8]](cite://8/1)[[9]](cite://9/1) The Tourist Department developed Tongariro as a visitor destination, building huts at Ketetahi and Waihohonu by 1904, and in 1929 the grand Chateau Tongariro hotel opened on the slopes of Mt Ruapehu. [[10]](cite://10/1)[[9]](cite://9/2)

This era was not without controversy. For a decade from 1914, Police Commissioner John Cullen spread tonnes of Scottish heather seed in Tongariro National Park to encourage grouse hunting — a move that drew sharp criticism from conservationists. [[9]](cite://9/3) Meanwhile, iwi involvement in park management was progressively diminished: after 1914, Tongariro was transferred from its founding trust board to the Tourist Department, and repeated requests for iwi recognition were refused for many years. [[11]](cite://11/1)

## The National Parks Act 1952: A New Framework

The post-war period brought a significant shift. Groups such as the Forest and Bird Society and the Federated Mountain Clubs argued for centralised control of the parks, and this movement culminated in the landmark National Parks Act 1952. [[12]](cite://12/1)

The new law established the National Parks Authority to provide guidance and policy, with boards overseeing individual parks alongside the Department of Lands and Survey. Crucially, the Act emphasised that native plants and animals would be preserved, and introduced species controlled or exterminated. [[12]](cite://12/2)

The 1950s and 1960s became something of a golden age for the parks. The number of national parks quickly grew from four to ten within a few years of the Act's passing. [[13]](cite://13/1) The New Zealand Forest Service entered the picture in 1954 with the first State Forest Park — Tararua — offering an alternative model of protected land management. [[13]](cite://13/2) The government also embarked on a massive programme of hut building, track cutting and footbridge construction: between 1957 and 1972, the Forest Service built 680 huts and shelters, 166 footbridges and cableways, and 4,000 kilometres of tramping tracks. [[13]](cite://13/3)

## Wilderness Areas: Protection Within Protection

As access to the backcountry improved, conservationists began to worry that the wildness of remote New Zealand was being tamed by overdevelopment. The answer was the creation of designated Wilderness Areas — places free of huts, tracks, bridges, and even helicopter access. [[13]](cite://13/4)

The first wilderness area, Otehake (12,000 hectares) in Arthur's Pass National Park, was established in 1955. [[14]](cite://14/1) By 1974, the first large wilderness areas — Pembroke, near Milford Sound, and Glaisnock (125,000 hectares) — were created in Fiordland National Park. [[15]](cite://15/1) A national wilderness conference held at Rotoiti Lodge in Nelson Lakes National Park in 1981 helped formalise policy, at which point there were seven wilderness areas, all within national parks. [[15]](cite://15/2)

From 1988, wilderness areas were also created outside the national park system, including the 40,000-hectare Raukumara on the East Cape and the 87,000-hectare Tasman in what is now Kahurangi National Park. [[16]](cite://16/1) By 2006, New Zealand had 11 wilderness areas in total. [[16]](cite://16/2)

## Legislative Evolution and the Department of Conservation

The National Parks Act 1980 added ecological systems to the list of features meriting national park status, and allowed for "specially protected areas" within parks to guard against harmful human activity. [[17]](cite://17/1) Then in 1987, the Department of Conservation (DOC) was established, and its founding act referenced the Treaty of Waitangi — leading to greater consultation with iwi across all parks and reserves. [[17]](cite://17/2)

In 1990, the National Parks Authority and park boards were abolished, replaced by the New Zealand Conservation Authority and local conservation boards. [[18]](cite://18/1) These new bodies were made responsible for all conservation land, balancing public access with the need to protect plants, animals and natural features, and placing restrictions on buildings, roads, vehicles and aircraft. [[19]](cite://19/1)

## New Parks and Māori Recognition

The later decades of the 20th century saw further additions to the network. Kahurangi National Park — New Zealand's 13th national park — was established in 1995 after years of lobbying, having faced significant opposition from mining and development interests. [[20]](cite://20/1) Abel Tasman National Park had been created much earlier, in 1942, to mark the tercentenary of Abel Tasman's arrival in New Zealand, largely through the advocacy of Nelson conservationist Perrine Moncrieff. [[20]](cite://20/2)

A landmark moment for Māori came in 2014, when Te Urewera National Park was disestablished and the land recognised as a legal entity in its own right — with mana (authority) and mauri (life force) — and Tūhoe confirmed as its guardians and governors. This represented a transformative model for incorporating Indigenous worldviews into New Zealand's conservation policy. [[21]](cite://21/1)

Today, New Zealand has 13 national parks, protecting some of the country's most spectacular landscapes — from the glaciers of Westland Tai Poutini and the limestone caves of Kahurangi to the volcanic peaks of Tongariro and the fiords of Fiordland. [[21]](cite://21/2)[[1]](cite://1/2) With 1.7 million overseas visitors recorded in 2017 alone, the parks remain central to both New Zealand's identity and its economy. [[21]](cite://21/3)
